solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cold listener dressing in coat, say?

indicators.note: one word dressing another wraps round it, so the word for cold goes around 'in'

parts.note: raw weather is cold and damp
the ear is the organ you listen with

explanation.surface: Someone with a chill and an ear problem is putting a dressing on it while wearing a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold listener' reads as one sick ear, but it is two pieces, and 'dressing' wraps the first round 'in'. The question mark flags that a coat is just one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A raincoat is one example of the clothing worn to keep off wet weather.

clue.text: Couple of scoundrels, second of which knocking out a tool

parts.note: a rat is a scoundrel, the first of the couple

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it from the word

parts.note: the second scoundrel is a cheat

explanation.surface: Two villains, the second knocking someone out with a tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking out' drops the A from CHEAT to give CHET.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a toothed mechanism, and also a spanner using one, so it is a tool.

clue.text: Fury in Liberian uprising

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so backwards
the letters are found inside the word

explanation.surface: Anger in a revolt in Liberia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' finds ERI inside Liberian; 'uprising' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is anger, a near-synonym of fury.

clue.text: Boat in current fix over foreign waters

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece over another comes before it

parts.note: wind is a current of air
a jam is a fix or difficult position
mer is French for sea

explanation.surface: A boat caught in a current gets into trouble in waters abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' is moving air rather than water.
explanation.definitionFit: A windjammer is a large merchant sailing ship, so a kind of boat.

clue.text: A team order that's generally accepted

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: a thing that is generally accepted

parts.note: XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team
OM is the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: An instruction to a side that everyone accepts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' is an honour, the British Order of Merit.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a statement taken as true without proof, so one everyone accepts.

clue.text: Drawn, revolutionary illustrations on Christmas cards, possibly?

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns right round, so the pieces are read backwards
in an across clue, one piece on another follows it

parts.note: Christmas falls in December, abbreviated Dec
illustrations are art

explanation.surface: A radical comments on the pictures printed on Christmas cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reverses DECART. 'cards, possibly' just pictures where December art appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture traced has been drawn by copying its outline, so the two past participles match.

clue.text: Part of cylinder coming out of trap?

indicators.note: trap is slang for mouth, so something coming out of it is spoken aloud

parts.note: a roll is a cylinder of rolled material

explanation.surface: A cylinder emerges from a trap, perhaps in a machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trap' is slang for the mouth, so the word is said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's role is the part they play.

clue.text: Fail — as may loose dentures?

definitions.meaning: dentures that are loose literally ... from the gums

explanation.surface: Failing, the way loose false teeth might.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming unstuck is idiom for collapsing or failing, and loose false teeth physically detach.

clue.text: Reportedly, brown square finished

indicators.note: reportedly means as said aloud, so the words are said aloud

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish brown; four is a square number, two times two

explanation.surface: Word has it a brown plaza is complete.
explanation.walkthrough: DUN FOUR spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be done for is idiom for being ruined or doomed, so finished.

clue.text: Superb striker cutting wood

indicators.note: one piece cutting another goes into it

parts.note: fir is a wood
a vesta is an old word for a match, something struck

explanation.surface: A fine footballer chops down a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striker' looks like a footballer but is a match; 'cutting' puts VESTA in FIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Five-star is a top rating as given to hotels, so it means excellent.

clue.text: Relative kidnapped by thin, mean and vile criminal in book

indicators.note: someone kidnapped is held inside by the captors, so one piece goes within the other
criminal suggests something bent or crooked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: SIB is short for sibling, a relative

explanation.surface: A family member is snatched by a gang of thin, mean, vile crooks in a thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges the three adjectives into THEINVILEMAN, which surrounds the sibling. The definition is H. G. Wells's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Invisible Man is a novel by H. G. Wells, so it is a book.

clue.text: Great, top athlete

parts.note: high can mean great, as in high hopes
a jumper is a top, the British word for a knitted sweater

explanation.surface: Praise for a first-class sportsperson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' looks like praise but is a garment: in Britain a jumper is a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A high jumper is a track-and-field competitor who leaps over a bar.

clue.text: Nail excellent start

parts.note: to nail someone is to catch or get them
cracking is British slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A first-rate opening as a nail goes in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nail' means catch, as in nail a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: To get cracking is idiom for starting work promptly.

clue.text: Crummy pudding

definitions.meaning: British slang for useless or of poor quality
a ... is a boiled pudding, as in plum ...

explanation.surface: A poor dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses duff for shoddy, and plum duff is a traditional boiled suet dessert.

clue.text: Sweet, soft lump, goalkeeper

parts.note: a gob is a soft lump of something slimy
a goalkeeper's job is to stop shots, so he is a stopper

explanation.surface: A list describing a goalkeeper: kind, soft and lumpish.
explanation.walkthrough: A gobstopper is a large hard British sweet that fills the mouth (gob).
explanation.definitionFit: A gobstopper is a big hard round candy, so a sweet in the British sense.

clue.text: Representative I came across in bed, retired

indicators.note: something retired has gone back, so the whole is read backwards
these words go inside the word for a bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
met means came across someone

explanation.surface: An agent describes bumping into someone in bed after going to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts IMET inside COT to give CIMETOT, which 'retired' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something totemic serves as an emblem, standing for and so representing a wider group.

clue.text: Minister reduced by hack's comic verse

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a cleric is a minister of religion
to hew is to hack

explanation.surface: A clergyman is taken down by a journalist's funny poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' looks like a journalist but is the verb to chop.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a four-line humorous biographical poem, a form of light verse.

clue.text: Lift in holiday centre going the wrong way, uncle's head stuck in it

indicators.note: one piece stuck in another sits inside it
travelling in the wrong direction, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a resort is a holiday centre

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An uncle gets his head trapped in a hotel lift that went the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going the wrong way' turns RESORT into TROSER; 'stuck in it' puts U inside. 'Lift' means steal, as does British slang trouser (pocket).
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly, so it means to steal.

clue.text: Seem discombobulated by twisting of Polish language

indicators.note: twisting the word round reads it backwards

parts.note: to polish is to rub

indicators.note: discombobulated means confused, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone appears baffled by a Polish twist of phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisting of' turns RUB into BUR; 'discombobulated' rearranges SEEM into MESE. 'Polish' is the verb, not the nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: Burmese is the official tongue of Myanmar, formerly Burma.

clue.text: Plain land for Conservative statesman

parts.note: bald means plain or unadorned, as in a bald statement
to land a prize is to win it

explanation.surface: A Tory politician gets flat country.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley Baldwin was three times Conservative Prime Minister of Britain between the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Baldwin led the Conservative Party and served as British Prime Minister.

clue.text: Echo a little bit, penetrating rupture

indicators.note: one piece penetrating another enters it, so it goes inside

parts.note: to rend is to tear apart or rupture
a sou was a French coin of small value, hence a tiny amount

explanation.surface: A small piece breaks into a tear and something reverberates.
explanation.walkthrough: The sou was an old French coin of tiny value, so 'a little bit' is a small sum; 'penetrating' sends it inside the tear.
explanation.definitionFit: To resound is to ring out and reverberate, which is what an echo does.

clue.text: Transfer tardy on ridiculously cheap excursion

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another follows it
to transfer is to move things to new places, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: 1P, one penny, is a ridiculously low price; the figure 1 stands in as the letter I

explanation.surface: A late arrival is moved onto an absurdly cheap outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transfer' looks like a coach transfer but rearranges TARDY into DAYTR. 1P is one penny, with the digit read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A day trip is an outing that goes and returns within one day, so it is an excursion.

clue.text: Lap pace

definitions.meaning: a ... is a fast speed, as in at a fair ...

explanation.surface: A runner's circuit and speed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat laps milk with its tongue, and going at a lick is British idiom for moving at speed.

clue.text: Player is in current contest

indicators.note: the given word sits inside the abbreviation

parts.note: DC stands for direct current
to jockey is to compete for advantage, as in jockeying for position

explanation.surface: A sportsman is taking part in the latest competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a sportsman, but it is someone playing records.
explanation.definitionFit: A DJ plays recorded music for radio listeners or a club, so a player of records.

clue.text: Lovely metal link

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a tie is a link

explanation.surface: A beautiful metal chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovely' is a noun here, an attractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutie is an attractive person, as a lovely is in older slang.

clue.text: Up past midnight with all the others

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: after midnight it is late

explanation.surface: Awake after midnight with everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' looks like awake but reverses LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al. is Latin shorthand meaning and others, used after a list of names.

clue.text: Game spelt out or encrypted in series of calls

parts.note: whist is a card game

indicators.note: encrypted text has its letters scrambled into code

explanation.surface: The name of a game is either written out in full or put into code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encrypted' rearranges SPELT OUT OR into LESTOPTOUR. 'calls' are visits, not phone calls.
explanation.definitionFit: A whistle-stop tour is a rapid trip with brief stops at many places, like a campaigning politician's visits.

clue.text: Blade on another razor, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letters of the words

explanation.surface: A cutting edge on a second razor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blade' suggests a razor, but it is the flat end of an oar.
explanation.definitionFit: An oar's flat end is its blade, and rowers call oars blades.

clue.text: Head of government in Scottish town backed complaint

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the whole is reversed
the letter goes inside the town's name

parts.note: Elgin is a town in Moray, in north-east Scotland

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A government leader in a Scottish town supported a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts G inside ELGIN to make ELGGIN, which 'backed' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A niggle is a minor grumble or nagging worry, so a small complaint.

clue.text: Drunk portrayed having dispensed with last of sherry in tumbler when maudlin?

indicators.note: drunk means reeling and disordered, so these letters are scrambled
dispensing with something does without it, so a letter is dropped
the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A sozzled actor drops the sherry and weeps into a glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last of' sherry gives Y, which 'having dispensed with' drops from PORTRAYED; 'Drunk' rearranges PORTRAED.
explanation.definitionFit: A maudlin drinker is tearful and sentimental, so a tear may fall into the glass.
